messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark, Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kayla is a 19-year-old married woman of North American background who is currently unemployed and living with her husband in a mid-sized city. She was referred for psychological assessment following a sexual assault that occurred approximately eight months ago, and her PCL-5 score of 61 places her firmly in the severe range of post-traumatic symptomatology. What brought her finally to the clinic was not any single crisis but a slow accumulation of losses — the person she had been before the assault had become unrecognizable to her, and she had begun to fear that version of herself was gone permanently.

The assault took place on a late summer evening when Kayla had been walking home from a friend's apartment. A man she did not know approached her from behind in an alleyway; she recalls the smell of alcohol on him before she even turned around, and the sound of a motorcycle idling somewhere nearby as the encounter escalated into violence. At one point he shouted at her in Arabic — words she did not understand but whose tone she understood completely. The assault lasted several minutes. When it was over she was left on the ground, the motorcycle noise fading into the distance and the smell of alcohol still thick in the air.

In the weeks that followed, Kayla found that her memory of the event did not behave the way she expected memory to behave. It did not recede. Instead, certain sensory fragments — the rev of a motorcycle engine, the smell of alcohol on someone's breath at a family gathering, the sound of raised Arabic-speaking voices from a neighbouring television — could instantly collapse the distance between then and now, pulling the full memory back without warning. When those memories returned they carried their original sensory texture: she would hear, internally, the sounds from the alley, and find herself smelling what she had smelled that night, as though her nervous system had preserved the scene in complete fidelity. These triggered memories fed directly into a state of acute threat — she would find herself scanning the room, checking over her shoulder, pressing her back against walls in public spaces, and lying awake listening for sounds at the front door that might mean someone was trying to get in. The memory did not merely recall danger; it reinstated it, and her body responded accordingly.

The threat monitoring itself deepened the problem. In a state of hypervigilant alertness, ordinary sounds became suspicious, and the heightened arousal made intrusive recall more likely, not less — her nervous system primed to detect the very cues that would reactivate the memory. She came to believe that the world she had understood before the assault — one in which she could move through public space without being harmed — had been revealed as a fiction. She was certain, in a way she found difficult to articulate, that she had failed in some fundamental way; that another person, someone more capable, more alert, more something, would have prevented what happened to her. These appraisals — that the world was permanently unsafe and that she herself was diminished — kept threat perception elevated even on days when nothing external provoked it.

Over months, Kayla built her life around avoidance. She stopped going out after dark entirely. She avoided the anniversary of the assault by spending the day sedated with sleep. She had stopped looking at her own body in mirrors or when changing clothes, finding that any attention to her physical self brought the memory of the assault flooding back and confirmed, in some wordless way, her belief that she was no longer the person she had been. These strategies did bring short-term relief, but they also narrowed her world severely — she had not worked since the assault, had declined social invitations, and her husband had begun expressing concern about her isolation. Crucially, the avoidance prevented her from processing the memory in any integrated way, keeping it raw and easily triggered. By restricting her environment so tightly, she had also inadvertently ensured that when triggers did occur — a motorcycle passing the window, a neighbour's shouting — their impact was amplified by the contrast with the silence she had constructed around herself, and the old appraisals of helplessness rushed back in full force.

Kayla came to the clinic hoping, cautiously, that something might be recoverable — some version of a life that did not organize itself entirely around what had happened to her in that alley. What she feared most was that the therapist would confirm what she already half-believed: that she was right to think she was no longer capable, and that nothing would change.
